question.title: Content Filtering for Customer-Facing Agent
question.scenario: A financial services company deploys a Claude-powered customer support agent that answers questions about loan products. The agent has access to tools that can look up account balances and payment history. The team discovers that some users are crafting prompts that cause the agent to reveal internal system prompts and tool schemas. The architect needs to add guardrails without significantly increasing latency.
question.question-text: What is the MOST effective first line of defense against prompt injection that attempts to extract system prompt contents from this customer-facing agent?

choices.choice: Add a regex filter that blocks any user message containing the words "system prompt," "instructions," or "ignore"
Place clear boundaries in the system prompt instructing Claude never to reveal its instructions, combined with input classification that flags suspicious messages for additional scrutiny
Remove the system prompt entirely and encode all instructions in few-shot examples within the conversation history
Rate limit each user to one message per minute so they cannot iterate on injection attempts

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Effective prompt injection defense is layered, combining model-level instructions with input-level detection.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The most effective approach combines system prompt hardening (explicitly instructing Claude to never disclose its instructions) with an input classification layer that detects and flags suspicious injection-style messages. Regex-based blocklists (A) are trivially bypassed through paraphrasing, encoding, or foreign languages. Removing the system prompt (C) sacrifices the most powerful control mechanism and does not prevent extraction of few-shot examples. Rate limiting (D) slows attackers but does not prevent successful injection on the very first attempt. Layered defense addresses both the model's behavior and the input pipeline.

ul.li: Defense-in-depth for prompt injection typically includes: input classification (using a separate lightweight model or Claude itself), system prompt hardening, output filtering, and monitoring/alerting on anomalous outputs.
Claude's training makes it inherently resistant to many injection attempts, but explicit system prompt instructions reinforce this behavior and provide a clear contract for the model to follow.
Production systems should log flagged messages and review them to continuously improve detection heuristics and close emerging bypass techniques.

question.title: Safe Defaults for Autonomous Code Agent
question.scenario: An engineering team is building an autonomous coding agent that uses Claude to fix bugs in a monorepo. The agent can read files, write files, run tests, and execute shell commands. The team wants the agent to operate with minimal human intervention during off-hours, but a recent incident revealed that the agent executed "rm -rf" on a build directory that contained uncommitted work. The architect must redesign the agent's safety boundaries.
question.question-text: Which guardrail design BEST balances autonomous operation with safety for this coding agent?

choices.choice: Maintain an allowlist of permitted shell commands and file paths, require human approval for any operation outside the allowlist, and enforce a read-only mode as the default that the agent must explicitly escalate out of
Log all agent actions for post-hoc review but allow unrestricted execution to maximize throughput
Restrict the agent to read-only operations only, requiring a human to apply all suggested changes manually
Run all commands inside a sandbox container with no network access and auto-approve everything

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Safe defaults mean restricting by default and explicitly granting elevated permissions, not the other way around.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: An allowlist-based approach with safe defaults (read-only by default, explicit escalation for writes/deletes) directly addresses the incident while preserving autonomy for known-safe operations. Logging without restrictions (B) detects problems only after damage occurs. Full read-only mode (C) eliminates the agent's ability to fix bugs autonomously, defeating its purpose. A sandbox with auto-approve (D) still allows destructive operations within the container and does not teach the agent boundaries -- if the sandbox includes the real repo checkout, the damage is real. The allowlist approach provides the principle of least privilege while maintaining useful autonomy.

ul.li: The principle of least privilege applied to AI agents means: start with zero permissions and grant only what is needed, with destructive operations requiring explicit escalation or human approval.

Allowlists are strictly preferred over denylists for agent tool access because denylists cannot anticipate every dangerous command, while allowlists fail-safe by blocking anything not explicitly permitted.

Production coding agents often implement tiered permission levels: read (default), write to known paths (auto-approved), write to unknown paths (requires approval), delete/execute (always requires approval or is prohibited).

question.title: Output Validation for Safety
question.scenario: A healthcare company uses Claude to summarize patient intake forms and generate preliminary triage notes for nurses. Regulatory compliance requires that the system never produces a definitive diagnosis or treatment recommendation, only summaries and flags for human review. The current system sometimes generates language like "the patient should be prescribed..." despite system prompt instructions.
question.question-text: What is the MOST reliable way to ensure the system's outputs comply with the regulatory constraint against generating treatment recommendations?

choices.choice: Increase the specificity of the system prompt to say "absolutely never generate treatment recommendations under any circumstances"
Use a lower temperature setting to reduce the chance of generating non-compliant output
Implement a post-generation output classifier that detects prescriptive medical language and blocks or rewrites non-compliant responses before they reach the user
Fine-tune Claude specifically for this use case to avoid generating medical recommendations

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When regulatory compliance is at stake, relying solely on prompt instructions is insufficient -- you need a programmatic enforcement layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A post-generation output classifier provides a deterministic, auditable safety layer that catches non-compliant outputs regardless of how or why the model generated them. System prompt improvements (A) reduce but cannot eliminate violations because language models are probabilistic. Lower temperature (B) reduces randomness but does not prevent systematic patterns. Fine-tuning (D) is expensive, unavailable for Claude through the standard API, and still cannot guarantee zero violations. The output classifier approach is the industry standard for regulated environments because it provides a hard boundary that is independent of model behavior.

ul.li: Defense-in-depth for regulated outputs typically combines: system prompt constraints, output classification/filtering, human review for edge cases, and audit logging of all generated content and filter decisions.
Output classifiers can range from keyword/regex detectors to separate Claude calls that evaluate compliance, depending on the required precision and latency budget.
In healthcare, the output filter should err on the side of blocking borderline content and escalating to human review rather than allowing potentially non-compliant language through.

question.title: Escalation to Human Reviewers
question.scenario: A large e-commerce company has deployed a Claude-powered agent that handles refund requests. The agent can autonomously approve refunds up to $50 and generate templated responses. For requests over $50 or those involving suspected fraud, the agent should escalate to a human reviewer. The team notices that the agent sometimes approves borderline cases autonomously when the user is persistent, and other times escalates trivially simple low-value requests unnecessarily.
question.question-text: Which design change would MOST effectively improve the escalation accuracy of this refund agent?

choices.choice: Add more emphatic language to the system prompt telling Claude to "strictly follow the $50 rule no matter what"
Remove the agent's ability to approve any refunds and route all requests to human reviewers

Implement the escalation decision as a programmatic rule in the orchestration layer based on structured data extracted by Claude, rather than letting Claude make the escalation decision in natural language
Train the agent with examples of persistent users so it learns to resist social pressure

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Separate data extraction (what Claude is good at) from policy enforcement (what code is good at).

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Moving the escalation decision into deterministic code in the orchestration layer ensures that policy rules (refund amount thresholds, fraud signals) are enforced consistently regardless of conversational pressure. Claude's role becomes extracting structured data (refund amount, reason, fraud indicators) which the orchestrator then evaluates against hard-coded rules. Emphatic prompting (A) is unreliable against persistent or cleverly phrased requests. Removing all autonomy (B) eliminates the agent's value proposition. Training with examples (D) may help but cannot guarantee deterministic policy compliance. The key insight is that business rules should live in code, not in prompts.

ul.li: The "extract then decide" pattern is a foundational principle in production agent design: use the LLM for understanding and extraction, use deterministic code for policy enforcement and routing.
This architecture is also more auditable -- you can log both the extracted data and the rule evaluation separately, making it easy to diagnose why any particular case was escalated or approved.
Anthropic recommends using tool-use responses with defined schemas to enforce structured extraction, which naturally separates the extraction step from the decision step.

question.title: Retry Strategy for Claude API Errors
question.scenario: A developer is integrating Claude into a CI/CD pipeline that reviews pull requests. The integration occasionally fails with HTTP 529 (overloaded) errors during peak hours. The developer wants to add retry logic to improve reliability without overwhelming the API.
question.question-text: Which retry strategy is MOST appropriate for handling Claude API overload (529) errors in a production integration?

choices.choice: Retry immediately with no delay, up to 10 times, to get through as quickly as possible
Fail immediately on the first 529 error and alert the developer to retry manually
Wait exactly 60 seconds between each retry to guarantee the API has recovered
Exponential backoff with jitter, starting at 1-2 seconds and capping at 60 seconds, with a maximum of 3-5 retries

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Exponential backoff with jitter is the standard pattern for handling transient overload errors in distributed systems.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Exponential backoff with jitter is the correct approach because it gradually increases the wait time between retries (reducing pressure on an overloaded service) while the jitter component prevents multiple clients from retrying in synchronized bursts (the "thundering herd" problem). Immediate retries (A) worsen the overload. Failing immediately (B) provides poor user experience for a transient condition. Fixed 60-second waits (C) are unnecessarily slow for transient issues and still lack jitter. The combination of exponential backoff, jitter, and a reasonable retry cap balances reliability with responsible API usage.

ul.li: Anthropic's API returns 529 for overload (distinct from 429 rate-limit). Both warrant retries, but 429 responses often include a Retry-After header that should be respected.
Jitter is critical in multi-client scenarios: without it, all clients that failed at the same time will retry at the same time, recreating the overload condition.
A common formula is: delay = min(cap, base * 2^attempt) + random(0, base), where base is typically 1 second and cap is 30-60 seconds.

question.title: Idempotent Tool Calls in Multi-Step Agents
question.scenario: A multi-agent research system uses Claude to gather data from external APIs, synthesize findings, and write reports. The agent executes tool calls to query databases and POST results to a reporting service. During a network interruption, the orchestrator loses connection mid-workflow and must resume. Some tool calls may have already executed successfully but the orchestrator did not receive confirmation. The architect must ensure resumption does not cause duplicate side effects.
question.question-text: Which design pattern BEST ensures safe resumption of this multi-step workflow without duplicate side effects?

choices.choice: Re-run the entire workflow from the beginning, since Claude will generate the same tool calls deterministically
Set the Claude API temperature to 0 to guarantee identical outputs on replay, then re-run from the start
Skip all tool calls that might have executed and only run the remaining steps, accepting possible gaps in data
Assign a unique idempotency key to each tool call, persist the key and result before execution, and on resume check whether each tool call has already completed before executing it

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Idempotency keys let you safely retry operations without worrying about duplicating side effects.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Assigning unique idempotency keys to each tool call and persisting their execution state creates a checkpoint system that allows safe resumption. On recovery, the orchestrator checks each tool call's key: if already executed, it reuses the stored result; if not, it executes normally. Re-running from scratch (A) is unsafe because Claude is not deterministic (even at temperature 0, outputs are not guaranteed identical) and because external APIs may create duplicates. Temperature 0 (B) does not guarantee determinism due to batching and floating-point differences, and even if it did, the external API calls would still duplicate. Skipping potentially-executed calls (C) loses data integrity.

ul.li: The idempotency pattern for agent tool calls follows the same principle as payment processing: write-ahead logging of intent, execution, and confirmation creates a recoverable state machine.
For read-only tool calls (database queries), idempotency is naturally safe -- the key concern is write operations (POSTs, updates, deletes) where duplication causes real harm.

Production agent frameworks often implement a "tool execution ledger" that records: tool name, parameters hash, idempotency key, execution status, and result -- enabling both safe retry and full audit trails.

question.title: Graceful Degradation When Claude Is Unavailable
question.scenario: A developer productivity platform uses Claude to provide real-time code suggestions as developers type. During a regional cloud outage, the Claude API becomes unreachable for approximately 15 minutes. The product manager wants to ensure developers can continue working without disruption. The architect is designing the degradation strategy.
question.question-text: Which graceful degradation strategy is MOST appropriate for this real-time code suggestion feature during a Claude API outage?

choices.choice: Queue all suggestion requests and replay them when the API recovers, delivering all suggestions at once
Show an error dialog every time a suggestion fails, so the developer knows exactly what is happening
Fall back to locally cached common suggestions or a simpler static autocomplete engine, with a subtle indicator that AI suggestions are temporarily unavailable
Switch to a different LLM provider automatically by maintaining hot-standby connections to multiple providers

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Graceful degradation means providing reduced but functional service, not no service or error spam.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Falling back to a simpler local suggestion engine maintains the developer's workflow with reduced quality rather than complete disruption. Queuing requests (A) is pointless for real-time suggestions -- by the time they are processed, the developer has moved on, and the context is stale. Showing error dialogs on every keystroke (B) is disruptive and provides no value. Maintaining hot-standby connections to alternative providers (D) adds significant complexity, cost, and prompt compatibility challenges, and is typically not justified for a suggestion feature. The best degradation maintains the user experience at reduced quality while clearly communicating the temporary limitation.

ul.li: Graceful degradation should be designed per-feature based on latency sensitivity: real-time features need instant fallbacks (local/cached), while batch features can queue and retry.

Circuit breaker patterns complement graceful degradation: after N consecutive failures, stop calling the API entirely and serve fallback responses, then periodically test whether the API has recovered.

The fallback quality level should be determined at design time -- teams should ask "what is the minimum useful experience we can provide without the AI?" and build that path proactively, not reactively.

question.title: Partial Failure in Multi-Step Extraction
question.scenario: A structured data extraction pipeline processes incoming contracts by sending each contract to Claude in three sequential steps: (1) extract party names and dates, (2) extract financial terms, (3) extract obligations and deadlines. Step 1 and Step 2 succeed, but Step 3 fails with a 500 Internal Server Error after two retries. The pipeline processes hundreds of contracts per day and must maintain high throughput.
question.question-text: How should the pipeline handle this partial failure scenario?

choices.choice: Discard all results from Steps 1 and 2 and re-queue the entire contract for reprocessing from scratch
Save the successful results from Steps 1 and 2 with a status marker indicating Step 3 is incomplete, place the contract in a retry queue for Step 3 only, and proceed to the next contract
Return the partial results from Steps 1 and 2 as the final output and mark the contract as complete
Halt the entire pipeline until the 500 error is resolved to prevent any incomplete data from being stored

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Checkpoint-and-resume patterns save completed work and retry only the failed step.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Saving partial results with a clear status marker and retrying only the failed step is the optimal approach. It preserves the work already done (avoiding redundant API calls and costs), maintains data integrity through explicit status tracking, and keeps the pipeline moving for other contracts. Discarding all results (A) wastes successful work and increases API costs. Marking incomplete data as complete (C) silently loses information and violates data integrity. Halting the entire pipeline (D) lets one failure block all other processing, which is unacceptable at high throughput. The checkpoint pattern enables both efficiency and correctness.

ul.li: Production extraction pipelines should model each document as a state machine with explicit states: queued, step-1-complete, step-2-complete, complete, and failed-at-step-N -- enabling targeted retries and progress monitoring.
A dead-letter queue should capture contracts that fail repeatedly (after max retries), routing them to human review rather than retrying indefinitely.
500 errors from the Claude API indicate a server-side issue and are transient -- they are safe to retry, unlike 400-level errors which typically indicate a problem with the request itself.

question.title: When to Require Human Approval
question.scenario: A company is deploying a Claude-powered agent for internal IT operations. The agent can reset passwords, provision new accounts, modify access control lists, and answer general IT questions. The security team needs to define which actions require human approval and which can be fully autonomous.
question.question-text: Which categorization of actions into autonomous vs. human-approved BEST reflects security best practices for this IT operations agent?

choices.choice: All actions autonomous -- the agent has the same permissions as an IT administrator
All actions require human approval -- the agent only drafts actions for a human to execute
Read-only queries and password resets are autonomous; account provisioning and ACL modifications require human approval
Actions are autonomous during business hours and require approval outside business hours

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Classify actions by their blast radius: low-risk reversible actions can be autonomous, high-risk or hard-to-reverse actions need human oversight.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Security best practices dictate that the approval requirement should be based on the risk and reversibility of each action, not on time-of-day or blanket policies. Read-only queries have zero blast radius and password resets are easily reversible and self-service -- both are safe for autonomous execution. Account provisioning creates new access surfaces and ACL modifications can escalate privileges, making both high-risk actions that warrant human review. Full autonomy (A) exposes the organization to agent errors on critical operations. Full manual mode (B) negates the agent's value. Time-based policies (D) have no security rationale -- a misconfigured ACL is equally dangerous at 2 PM and 2 AM.

ul.li: The "blast radius" framework for agent permissions considers: reversibility (can the action be undone?), scope (how many systems/users are affected?), sensitivity (does it involve credentials or access control?), and auditability (is there a clear trail?).
Even autonomous actions should be logged with full context (who triggered, what parameters, what result) to maintain an audit trail for compliance.
As trust in the agent grows over time, the boundary between autonomous and human-approved can shift -- but this should be a deliberate, documented security decision, not an organic drift.

question.title: Confidence Thresholds for Escalation
question.scenario: A legal technology company has built a Claude-based contract review agent that identifies risky clauses and classifies them by severity (low, medium, high). The agent processes thousands of contracts per week. The legal team wants to review only the contracts that truly need human attention, but they cannot afford to miss genuinely high-risk clauses. The team is debating how to set the confidence threshold for escalation to human review.
question.question-text: Which threshold strategy BEST balances thoroughness with reviewer efficiency for this contract review system?

choices.choice: Set a single high confidence threshold (e.g., 95%) -- only escalate when the agent is very confident a clause is high-risk, minimizing the volume of human reviews
Escalate everything classified as medium or high risk regardless of confidence, ensuring humans see all potentially risky clauses

Use asymmetric thresholds: escalate high-risk classifications at a low confidence bar (e.g., 60%) to avoid missing dangers, but require high confidence (e.g., 90%) before autonomously marking a contract as low-risk and skipping human review
Let the legal team manually set thresholds per contract type without providing a default, since risk tolerance varies

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When the cost of a false negative (missing a real risk) far exceeds the cost of a false positive (unnecessary review), thresholds should be asymmetric.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Asymmetric thresholds correctly reflect the asymmetric costs in legal review. Missing a genuinely high-risk clause (false negative) could expose the company to significant legal liability, so the bar for escalation should be low -- even moderate suspicion warrants human eyes. Conversely, the bar for autonomously clearing a contract should be high, because incorrectly skipping review is the dangerous failure mode. A single high threshold (A) optimizes for reviewer efficiency at the cost of safety. Escalating everything medium+ (B) overwhelms reviewers and defeats the purpose of automation. Deferring entirely to per-type manual configuration (D) provides no safe default and risks misconfiguration.

ul.li: Asymmetric thresholds mirror the concept of "sensitivity vs. specificity" in medical testing -- for high-consequence domains, you optimize for sensitivity (catching all true positives) even at the cost of more false positives.

The confidence scores from Claude can be obtained by asking the model to rate its confidence explicitly in a structured response, or by analyzing logprobs where available -- but these should be calibrated against ground truth before relying on specific numeric thresholds.

Over time, the thresholds can be tuned using feedback data: track which escalated contracts actually required human intervention and which were false alarms, then adjust thresholds to optimize the precision-recall tradeoff for the specific domain.

question.title: Feedback Loops for Agent Improvement
question.scenario: A customer support team uses a Claude-powered agent that drafts responses to support tickets. Human agents review each draft, edit it if needed, and send the final version. After three months, the team wants to use the accumulated human edits to improve the agent's drafts. The architect is designing the feedback loop.
question.question-text: Which feedback loop design will MOST effectively improve the agent's draft quality over time?

choices.choice: Collect all human edits and add them as few-shot examples in the system prompt, replacing the oldest examples as the prompt grows too long
Fine-tune Claude on the corrected responses to permanently encode the team's preferences into the model
Automatically accept any draft that a human agent sends without editing, and only flag drafts that required significant changes for review

Track edit patterns to identify systematic issues (e.g., tone adjustments, missing information types), then update the system prompt instructions to address those specific patterns, and use representative before/after pairs as few-shot examples

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Effective feedback loops identify patterns in corrections rather than treating each edit as an independent example.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Analyzing edit patterns to identify systematic issues and then updating prompt instructions is the most effective and sustainable approach. It converts raw data (individual edits) into actionable insights (instruction improvements) and targeted examples. Dumping all edits as few-shot examples (A) does not scale -- prompt context is limited, and raw examples without analysis may contain contradictions or noise. Fine-tuning (B) is not available through Claude's standard API, is expensive, and creates a static improvement that does not adapt to changing needs. Tracking unedited drafts (C) only identifies when the agent is "good enough" but does not provide direction for improvement.

ul.li: The most impactful feedback loop improvements typically come from identifying the top 3-5 systematic error categories (e.g., "too formal," "misses refund eligibility check," "does not acknowledge customer frustration") and addressing each with targeted prompt instructions.

Few-shot examples should be curated, not accumulated -- select the most representative and instructive before/after pairs that illustrate the desired corrections, and rotate them based on current error patterns.

Measuring improvement requires tracking the edit rate and edit magnitude over time, segmented by issue type, to confirm that prompt changes actually reduce specific error categories rather than merely shifting errors elsewhere.

question.title: Approval Workflows for High-Risk Actions
question.scenario: A financial services firm uses a Claude-powered agent that generates and sends client communications, including portfolio updates and trade confirmations. Regulatory requirements mandate that certain communications (those containing performance claims or forward-looking statements) must be reviewed by a compliance officer before being sent. The agent processes 500+ communications daily, and the compliance team has capacity for approximately 50 manual reviews per day.
question.question-text: Which approval workflow design BEST satisfies the regulatory requirement while respecting the compliance team's capacity constraints?

choices.choice: Route all 500+ communications through compliance review, hiring additional compliance officers to handle the volume

Have Claude classify each communication as "contains regulated content" or "routine," auto-send routine messages, and route only regulated messages to compliance review, with sampling-based audits of auto-sent messages
Auto-send all communications and conduct weekly batch reviews of a random sample to check compliance
Allow the agent to self-certify compliance by including a confidence score, and only escalate messages where the score is below 50%

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Use the AI to triage which messages need human review, while maintaining audit mechanisms to verify the triage accuracy.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Having Claude classify communications and routing only regulated content to compliance review directly addresses both constraints: it satisfies the regulatory requirement by ensuring regulated communications are reviewed before sending, while respecting the team's 50-review-per-day capacity by filtering out routine messages. The sampling-based audit of auto-sent messages provides a safety net to catch classification errors. Reviewing everything (A) is infeasible at current capacity. Weekly batch reviews (C) violate the "before being sent" requirement. Self-certification with a low threshold (D) provides no human oversight and would not satisfy regulators -- the compliance officer review is the requirement, not optional.

ul.li: This "AI triage + human review" pattern is common in regulated industries: the AI handles volume reduction and routing, while humans provide the authoritative compliance decision on flagged items.

The sampling audit serves two purposes: it catches systematic classification errors (e.g., if Claude consistently misclassifies a new type of performance claim) and it provides evidence to regulators that the automated routing is being monitored.

The classification itself should be conservative -- if in doubt, route to compliance -- because the cost of a missed regulated communication (regulatory penalty) far exceeds the cost of an unnecessary review (compliance officer time).

question.title: Chunking Strategy for Legal Documents
question.scenario: A legal analytics platform needs to extract key terms, obligations, and risk factors from commercial contracts that range from 20 to 200 pages. Claude's context window can handle approximately 150 pages of text. The architect must design a chunking strategy that works for all document sizes while maintaining extraction accuracy, especially for clauses that reference other sections of the contract (e.g., "subject to the indemnification provisions in Section 12.3").
question.question-text: Which chunking strategy BEST handles cross-reference dependencies while maintaining extraction accuracy?

choices.choice: For documents under 150 pages, process in a single pass; for longer documents, chunk by logical sections (e.g., articles/clauses) with overlapping context windows that include the table of contents and referenced sections, then reconcile extracted terms across chunks
Split the document into fixed-size chunks of 10 pages each with no overlap, process each independently, then merge results
Always split into the smallest possible chunks (1-2 pages each) to maximize parallelism and reduce per-call cost
Use only the first and last 50 pages of each contract, since key terms are typically in the preamble and schedules

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When the document fits in the context window, avoid chunking entirely. When chunking is necessary, respect the document's logical structure.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The optimal strategy avoids unnecessary chunking (single-pass for documents that fit) and uses intelligent, structure-aware chunking when needed. Chunking by logical sections preserves the semantic coherence of individual clauses. Including the table of contents and referenced sections in the overlap provides the cross-reference context that fixed-size chunking (B) destroys. Very small chunks (C) maximize the risk of splitting related content and lose cross-reference context entirely. Skipping middle sections (D) guarantees missing critical contract terms. The reconciliation step across chunks catches any extraction inconsistencies or duplicates from the overlap.

ul.li: Structure-aware chunking uses document landmarks (section headers, article numbers, page breaks with TOC references) rather than arbitrary character/token counts, preserving semantic units that the model can reason about coherently.

The "context primer" pattern -- including key metadata (table of contents, definitions section, party names) at the start of every chunk -- dramatically improves extraction accuracy by giving Claude the reference frame it needs to interpret section-specific language.

Reconciliation across chunks should handle: deduplication of terms extracted from overlapping regions, resolution of conflicting extractions (same clause interpreted differently in different chunks), and assembly of cross-referenced obligations into a coherent dependency graph.

question.title: Map-Reduce Pattern for Multi-Document Analysis
question.scenario: A research team needs to analyze 500 academic papers to identify consensus findings, contradictions, and research gaps in a specific domain. Each paper is 10-30 pages. The analysis requires Claude to read each paper, extract key findings with supporting evidence, and then synthesize a comprehensive literature review that cites specific papers. The architect must design a workflow that produces an accurate, well-cited synthesis without hallucinating citations.
question.question-text: Which workflow architecture MOST reliably produces an accurate, well-cited literature synthesis at this scale?

choices.choice: Concatenate all 500 paper abstracts into a single prompt and ask Claude to write the literature review in one pass

A three-phase map-reduce: (1) Map phase extracts structured findings with verbatim quotes and metadata from each paper individually; (2) Reduce phase clusters and cross-references findings by topic; (3) Synthesis phase generates the review using only the structured extractions as source material, with citation provenance tracked from phase 1 through to the final output
Process papers in batches of 50, generate a partial synthesis for each batch, then ask Claude to merge all 10 partial syntheses into a final review
Send all papers to Claude with extended thinking enabled and a very large max_tokens value to handle the full analysis in a single call

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Citation accuracy requires provenance tracking from source document through every processing stage to the final output.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The three-phase map-reduce approach is the only option that maintains citation provenance throughout the entire pipeline. Phase 1 (map) creates structured, citable extractions from each paper with verbatim quotes that can be verified. Phase 2 (reduce) organizes findings without losing their source attribution. Phase 3 (synthesis) generates prose from verified extractions rather than from memory, dramatically reducing hallucination risk. Abstract-only analysis (A) loses the supporting evidence and nuance in the full papers. Batch processing with iterative merging (C) degrades citation accuracy at each merge step as context is compressed. A single massive call (D) exceeds Claude's context window by orders of magnitude -- 500 papers at 10-30 pages each is roughly 5,000-15,000 pages of text.

ul.li: The map phase should output structured records (paper ID, finding, verbatim supporting quote, page number, confidence level) that serve as a verifiable "evidence chain" -- any claim in the final synthesis can be traced back to a specific quote from a specific paper.

The reduce phase benefits from hierarchical clustering: first group by topic/subtopic, then within each cluster identify agreements, contradictions, and gaps. This structure directly maps to the sections of a literature review.

Hallucination prevention in synthesis relies on constraining Claude to reference only the structured extractions provided in its prompt -- it should never generate a citation it was not given, and the orchestrator should verify every cited paper ID in the output exists in the extraction database.

question.title: Maintaining Coherence Across Chunks
question.scenario: A publishing company uses Claude to proofread and provide editorial feedback on book manuscripts (200-400 pages). The manuscripts must be processed in chunks due to context window limits. Early testers report that feedback on later chapters sometimes contradicts advice given on earlier chapters, and the agent loses track of character names, plot points, and stylistic preferences established in previous chunks.
question.question-text: Which approach MOST effectively maintains coherence and consistency of editorial feedback across chunks of a long manuscript?

choices.choice: Maintain a running summary document that captures key context (character names, plot points, established style decisions, and prior feedback) and include it as a preamble in each subsequent chunk's prompt
Process each chunk independently and let the human editor resolve any inconsistencies across chunks
Process the manuscript backwards (last chapter first) so that the final pass covers the opening chapters where consistency matters most
Increase the chunk size to the maximum possible context window length to minimize the number of boundaries

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When processing sequentially, carry forward a compressed representation of prior context to inform each new chunk.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A running summary document acts as a "memory" that persists across chunk boundaries, giving Claude the context it needs to provide consistent feedback. This summary captures the essential information (characters, plot, style decisions, prior feedback) in a compact form that fits alongside each new chunk. Independent processing (B) guarantees inconsistency and pushes the burden to the human. Reverse processing (C) does not solve the coherence problem -- it simply moves the inconsistencies to different chapters. Maximizing chunk size (D) reduces but does not eliminate boundaries, and the largest chunks may leave too little room for the summary context and instructions in the prompt.

ul.li: The running summary should be structured (e.g., sections for characters, plot events, style guide, prior feedback decisions) rather than free-form prose, making it easier to update incrementally and for Claude to reference specific elements.

The summary should be updated after each chunk is processed, incorporating any new characters, plot developments, or style decisions -- this update step can itself be a Claude call that takes the previous summary and the current chunk's analysis as input.

For very long manuscripts, the summary may need its own compression strategy: less important details (minor characters, resolved subplots) can be condensed or removed to keep the summary within a manageable size, while critical information (main characters, unresolved conflicts, recurring style issues) is preserved at full detail.
